findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: A mutable URL is downloaded and piped directly to a root shell during every build. A compromised endpoint, DNS/TLS trust-chain failure, or changed installer can execute arbitrary code in the produced image without any reviewed or integrity-checked artifact.

findings.title: Pin and verify the remotely executed installer
findings.whyItBreaks: This downloads mutable network content and executes it as the image build user without a version pin or integrity check. A changed or compromised response can execute arbitrary build-time code and alter the shipped image.

findings.title: Make installer download failures fail the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: In a shell pipeline, the RUN status is the status of `sh`, not `curl`. If curl fails and writes no script, `sh` can exit successfully on empty input, so Docker can produce an image after a failed installation.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: A compromised origin, DNS/TLS trust path, or changed install.sh can execute arbitrary code during every image build. The URL has neither a version pin nor a checksum/signature verification.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error in the exported load API
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for absent keys, but this wrapper discards it and returns "", which is indistinguishable from a present key whose value is legitimately empty. Every caller of this exported API is forced to treat a failed lookup as real data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in the exported helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards it and returns "". A caller cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key whose value is intentionally empty, so it may treat missing data as a real value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures in the exported loader
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing when a key is absent, but this exported API discards that error and returns "". A caller cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key whose legitimate value is empty, so it can treat missing data as real data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every result had been delivered. The new goroutines may send after Run returns, so a caller that closes results after Run can cause a send-on-closed-channel panic; blocked sends can also leak goroutines. Result ordering is no longer preserved.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: The new untracked goroutines allow Run to return before any result is sent. Callers have no completion signal, so they cannot safely close or finish consuming results after Run returns; closing a caller-owned channel can panic in a late send, and result order/completion becomes nondeterministic.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now occurs in an untracked goroutine, so Run can return before any result is delivered. A caller that closes results after Run returns will nondeterministically panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also lose the prior completion guarantee.

findings.title: Require admin privileges for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || makes canDeleteRecord return true when a non-admin user's tenant matches the record tenant. This bypasses the existing administrator requirement and authorizes regular tenant users to delete records.

findings.title: Restore conjunctive tenant-admin authorization
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes a non-admin whenever the record shares their tenant, and authorizes an admin for records in any tenant. The prior predicate required both properties, so this is an authorization bypass on a destructive operation.

findings.title: Require admin status and tenant match before deleting records
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes any non-admin session whose tenant matches the record to delete it, and authorizes an admin from a different tenant. The previous conjunction enforced both privileges, so this expands deletion authority across users and tenant boundaries.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-settings failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid JSON or invalid settings formerly threw, preventing callers from treating corrupt input as valid. Now updateFontSize receives defaults, overwrites fontSize, and saves `{theme:"light",fontSize:size}`, silently replacing the user's malformed persisted data.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of returning defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts JSON syntax errors and invalid settings fields into a normal Settings value. updateFontSize therefore proceeds to save `{theme:"light",fontSize:size}` for malformed input, whereas it previously propagated the error and did not write. The exported parseSettings API also now forces callers to conflate invalid input with a legitimate default configuration.

findings.title: Preserve parse failure before saving updated settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts malformed or schema-invalid input into a real Settings value. updateFontSize then cannot distinguish that failure from genuine defaults and saves it. For example, updating the font size of {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"bad"} now persists theme "light", whereas the previous parse error prevented the write.

findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from the hard-coded "verified" ref, builtFrom identifies the requested branch commit but artifacts contains files from verified. Consumers receive a self-inconsistent BuildReport and can publish or display artifacts as belonging to the wrong commit.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom names the branch commit while artifacts are fetched from the verified commit. Consumers receive a self-inconsistent report and can publish or inspect artifacts from the wrong build.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom reports build.ref(branch) but artifacts are fetched from build.ref("verified"). Consumers receive a self-contradictory report and may attribute verified artifacts to the requested branch commit.

findings.title: Restore the positive limit cap
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, recentEntries now returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit. Consequently, renderFeed(all) passes 20 but iterates the unbounded result; assigning index 20 or later extends its initially 20-slot array, so feeds with more than 20 entries produce oversized pages.

findings.title: Restore enforcement of the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all entries rather than at most limit entries. For example, recentEntries(["a", "b"], 1) returns ["b", "a"]. The in-repo renderFeed caller supplies 20 but loops over page.length, so an input with 21 entries expands its 20-slot output array and returns 21 entries.

findings.title: Restore the positive-limit cap
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit, this returns every entry rather than at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 and allocates a 20-slot output, but its loop writes every returned entry; inputs with more than 20 entries expand the output beyond 20.

findings.title: Count emitted entries after filtering stale rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When any input entry is stale, rows contains only live entries while the unchanged header still receives entries.length. For example, one live and one stale entry emits one row but declares '# entry-count: 2', producing an internally inconsistent manifest for consumers that use the header to validate or parse its rows.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, the function omits its row but still emits `# entry-count` from `entries.length`. The resulting manifest claims more entries than it contains, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or parse its rows.

findings.title: Count only rendered entries in manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are omitted from rows, but `# entry-count` still uses `entries.length`. For one live and one stale entry, the manifest declares 2 entries but contains 1 row, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or parse the manifest.

findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported FormatLegacyID is a source-incompatible API change: any downstream package that calls ids.FormatLegacyID will fail to compile after upgrading, with no replacement or migration path provided.

findings.title: Retain the exported legacy-ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting exported FormatLegacyID is a source-compatible-breaking change for external users of example.com/app/ids: callers using ids.FormatLegacyID no longer compile, with no replacement or deprecation window.

findings.title: Restore the exported legacy ID formatter

findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported function from this module, but it is deleted rather than re-exported under its prior name. Any existing consumer importing shippingQuote from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: `shippingQuote` was an exported API in the base revision but is removed. Any existing consumer importing it from `src/orders` will fail to compile or load after upgrading, despite the quote behavior still existing under a new module and name.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute function now fails with an Error, so callers cannot receive the string promised by its return type; previously it returned the uppercased input.

findings.title: Restore execute's string-returning behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but every invocation now throws "always fails" and cannot produce a result. This replaces the prior uppercase transformation with an unusable public API.

findings.title: Restore execute's string-return contract

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, handle previously returned "read-only". The new eligibility gate returns false first, so handle at line 24 returns "rejected" and the viewer-specific branch at line 25 is unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve the active viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with remaining attempts now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" before reaching its existing viewer-specific "read-only" branch. Previously the same request returned "read-only".

findings.title: Preserve the read-only path for active viewers
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer previously passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only" at line 25. The added role gate makes the same request return "rejected" at line 24, blocking a role that has an explicit supported outcome.

findings.title: Do not require payment to save drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; a draft with `payment: "missing"` previously returns `"saved"` but now returns `"blocked"`. Payment should govern submission, not preservation of an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Keep payment checks out of draft saves
findings.whyItBreaks: The new payment requirement changes saveDraft({ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }) from "saved" to "blocked". Saving a draft is independently valid before payment, but it shares canProceed with submission.

findings.title: Keep payment validation out of draft saving
findings.whyItBreaks: The new payment requirement is shared by submitOrder and saveDraft. An order with state="draft" and payment="missing" now returns false from canProceed, so saveDraft returns "blocked" even though saving an unpaid draft must remain possible.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the requested channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When `channel` and `stable` point to different commits, the returned Snapshot reports the channel head in `commit` but contains the file list for `stable`. Consumers cannot reconstruct or trust the advertised snapshot.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, Snapshot.commit remains the requested channel's head while Snapshot.files is read from stable. Consumers therefore receive a snapshot whose file list does not describe its advertised commit/channel.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from `stable`, the returned snapshot reports that channel's commit but contains `stable`'s files. Consumers cannot reliably reconstruct or publish the stated commit; repositories without a `stable` ref also fail despite a valid requested channel.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `limit` promises to cap the returned items, but the body still unconditionally sets `max_count = 10`; `build("item", 3)` returns ten items rather than three.

findings.title: Honor the `limit` argument
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=10)` promises a caller-controlled result cap, but the body always assigns `max_count = 10`; therefore `build("x", 3)` still returns 10 items.

findings.title: Honor the `limit` parameter

findings.title: Validate positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public function promises a positive integer but returns int(value) unchanged. For example, charge('-1') now produces -100, so callers relying on the function name to enforce a positive amount can create negative charges.

findings.title: Validate that parsed amounts are strictly positive

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame instead of mutating it

findings.title: Serialize reservation updates across the persistence await

findings.title: Update retry to consume the millisecond backoff
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still multiplies that value by 1,000 before passing it to its millisecond-based sleep. A first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) instead of one second; higher attempts can wait up to 30,000,000,000 ms.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still multiplies that value by 1,000 before passing it to sleep. After the first failed attempt, retry waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) instead of the previous 1,000 ms; later retries are similarly delayed.

findings.title: Preserve milliseconds at the retry call site
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). A first retry waits 1,000,000 ms instead of the prior 1,000 ms; at the 30,000-ms cap it waits over 8 hours. Polling was updated to consume the new millisecond unit directly, so retries were missed during the unit migration.

findings.title: Propagate the final file close error

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. Previously, a successful flush returned f.Close()'s error, so callers could detect final file-write/close failures; Save now reports success in that case.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous success path returned f.Close()'s error. The new deferred close discards that error, causing Save to return nil after a successful buffered flush even if final filesystem write/close fails.

findings.whyItBreaks: `range(start, end - 1)` excludes index `end - 1`, so each non-empty page loses its last row. Consequently, render_page and summarize silently omit rows (including every single-row page).

findings.title: Include the page endpoint in page_window
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds end is excluded twice: range(start, end - 1) omits the final row of every non-empty page. A one-row page becomes empty, and render_page/summarize therefore silently lose data.

findings.title: Keep existing keyword argument names
findings.whyItBreaks: All public functions rename their parameters (for example page_count(total, size) to page_count(total_rows, page_size)). Existing keyword calls such as page_count(total=10, size=5) now raise TypeError instead of producing a result.

findings.title: Return entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition is inverted: a fresh entry with elapsed time below ttlMs is deleted and returns null, while an expired entry is returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice the array while iterating forward
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next element into the current index, but forEach then advances past it. For example, `[done, done, pending]` returns `[done, pending]`, leaving a completed job unpruned.

findings.title: Restore TTL cache hit semantics
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time 0 and is immediately deleted as a cache miss, while entries older than ttlMs are returned as cache hits. This reverses the public TtlCache/ttlMs contract.

findings.title: Filter all completed jobs without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach advances the index after removing an element. For [{done:true}, {done:true}], the second job shifts to index 0 but iteration proceeds to index 1, so pruneDone returns a completed job. The change also mutates the caller's input array, unlike the previous filter implementation.

findings.title: Return entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `>` comparison returns expired entries while deleting fresh entries. A value read immediately after `set` returns null, while a value older than `ttlMs` is served.

findings.title: Remove all completed jobs without skipping shifted entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during a forward `forEach` shifts the next job into the removed index, then `forEach` advances past it. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve zero for an empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: For averageAmount([]), total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN. The previous implementation returned 0, making empty datasets produce an invalid numeric result.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows. Previously busiest sorted a copy, so callers could retain their original ordering; now invoking busiest silently reorders their data.

findings.title: Preserve zero for an empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: For averageAmount([]), total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN. The prior implementation explicitly returned 0 for this supported input.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows. Calling busiest() now reorders the caller-owned input, unlike the previous copied-and-sorted implementation; later consumers can observe a different row order.

findings.title: Restore empty-input handling in averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, reduce returns 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the previous documented-by-behavior result of 0.

findings.title: Avoid mutating the caller's rows array in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. Previously busiest sorted a copy, so callers could retain their original ordering; this change silently reorders their data.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically in descending order
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort without a comparator sorts numbers as strings. For input scores [9, 100, 8] and n=1, this produces ranking [9, 8, 100], making the cutoff 9; filtering then returns both 9 and 100 and slice(0, 1) returns the 9-point player instead of the 100-point player.

findings.title: Restore numeric score comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() compares numbers as strings. For players ordered B=9, A=100, C=8, rankScores returns [9, 8, 100], so topPlayers(..., 1) uses cutoff 9 and returns B rather than the actual leader A.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores [8, 9, 100], rankScores returns [9, 8, 100]; with n=1, topPlayers uses cutoff 9 and can return the 9-score player before the 100-score player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using normal string equality can reveal how much of a supplied HMAC matches through response timing. An attacker able to make repeated requests can use that signal to forge a signature; verify() gates handle()'s 401 response versus processor execution.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Direct string equality can return sooner for signatures that differ earlier, exposing comparison timing to callers of the authentication path. An attacker able to make repeated requests can use this signal to progressively guess a valid HMAC signature; the prior hmac.compare_digest call was specifically designed to avoid this.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using == can return sooner when signatures differ earlier, exposing comparison timing to a remote caller. Because handle() uses this result to authorize webhook processing, an attacker can use timing observations to progressively forge a valid HMAC signature.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Exiting the transaction at line 23 commits the ledger record before `_apply_balances` runs. If either balance update fails or the process stops during line 24, the transfer is recorded as completed while one or both account balances were not updated; the previous implementation rolled all three writes back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after recording the ledger entry. If either subsequent balance UPDATE fails, the ledger permanently records a transfer that was not fully applied; if the second UPDATE fails, the source account may also be debited without crediting the destination.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the `with db.transaction()` block exits, before either balance update executes. If a balance update fails, the committed ledger entry remains; if the second update fails, the source account is debited without crediting the destination.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: For the same instant, the returned billing day now depends on the server's local timezone. For example, at 2024-01-01T00:30:00.000Z a UTC-08 host returns 2023-12-31, whereas the previous implementation returned 2024-01-01. This also changes sameBillingDay results around UTC midnight and can assign billing activity to the wrong day.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces the previous UTC-based public result with host-local calendar fields. For example, the same instant 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z now returns 2025-12-31 on a UTC-08 host but previously returned 2026-01-01 everywhere, changing billing grouping and sameBillingDay results based on deployment timezone.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces the previous explicit UTC getters with local-time getters. The same instant can now produce different billing days on hosts in different timezones—for example, a timestamp shortly after 00:00 UTC is assigned to the prior local calendar day in negative-offset zones. This also changes sameBillingDay results across deployment environments.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: A request for tenant A/account X stores its Profile under X; a later request for tenant B/account X returns tenant A's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile. This bypasses tenant isolation and exposes incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads account X, a request for tenant B and account X finds the same account-only key and returns tenant A's cached Profile at line 16. This bypasses the tenant-aware fetchProfile call and can disclose cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping to the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads account X, a read for tenant B/account X returns tenant A's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile. This exposes one tenant's profile data to another and returns an incorrect tenant value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: ...")`; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. The exported API and `loadAll` callers can therefore treat absent data as successfully loaded.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key now returns "" instead of throwing. Empty string is a valid Map value, so loadAll at line 12 silently produces data indistinguishable from a successfully loaded empty value; callers cannot detect incomplete input.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts the prior missing-key error into "". loadAll consequently returns an array containing an indistinguishable empty value for a missing key rather than failing, so callers can treat incomplete data as successfully loaded.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing retry configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported, but existing callers supplying the prior required { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } shape now fail TypeScript checking because timeoutMs was removed and retries and timeout became required. Existing serialized/config-driven consumers also no longer provide the field read at line 8.

findings.title: Propagate retryBackground's final callback failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly exported retryBackground catches every callback exception and returns void after retries or deadline expiry. Its callers therefore receive the identical successful return value for success, timeout, and exhausted failures, so they cannot avoid treating failed background work as completed.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config timeout contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers supply `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }`. They now fail TypeScript checking because `retries` and `timeout` are required; untyped consumers instead pass no `timeout`, so `Date.now() + undefined` becomes NaN and the deadline guard never expires.

findings.title: Expose terminal retry failure to retryBackground callers
findings.whyItBreaks: If every callback attempt throws, `retryBackground` catches each exception and returns `void`, exactly like a successful callback. As an exported API, this forces callers to treat an exhausted failure as success and prevents them from reporting or recovering from it.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields for retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and is consumed by the existing exported retry API. Existing TypeScript callers supplying { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } now fail to type-check because retries is required and timeoutMs was removed. Untyped callers compute Date.now() + undefined, yielding NaN, so retry silently stops enforcing its prior timeout.

findings.title: Implement retryBackground without blocking the caller
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported retryBackground name promises background execution, but it calls fn() synchronously before returning. A caller using this API to defer slow or blocking work instead blocks for every attempted invocation.

findings.title: Expose failure after background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from fn is discarded; after the final failed attempt retryBackground returns void, indistinguishable from successful completion. As an exported API, this forces all callers to treat permanent failure as success.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now publicly permits a number, but numbers have no `length`; passing `value={42}` produces `len=undefined` (and is rejected by TypeScript type checking).

findings.title: Handle numeric field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now permits `number`, but `number` has no `length`. Type-checking rejects this expression; if emitted without type checking, `<Field value={123} />` renders `len=undefined` rather than the intended length.

findings.title: Convert numeric values before reading their length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now accepts `number`, but numbers have no `length`. TypeScript rejects this expression, and transpile-only consumers render `len=undefined` for values such as `123`.

findings.title: Preserve the larger buffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: `git diff` at line 140 returns the entire PR patch, but `spawnSync` now uses Node's 1 MiB default maxBuffer. A patch exceeding that limit is terminated with a buffer error, `git()` throws, and the review posts a failed check instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore the Git diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `runGithub` reads the entire PR patch via `git diff` at line 140. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses Node's 1 MiB default; a larger diff returns an output-buffer error, so `git()` throws and the review reports failure instead of reviewing the PR. The removed 64 MiB limit previously supported these valid patches.

findings.title: Retain capacity for large Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `spawnSync` now uses Node's default `maxBuffer` of 1 MiB. The `git diff` call at line 140 reads the complete PR patch, so a patch exceeding that size terminates with a buffer error and the review fails before producing results. The prior 64 MiB limit supported these PRs.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: This public helper runs Codex with opts.repoPath as its working directory. Removing `-s read-only` means model-generated shell commands now use the CLI's configured/default sandbox instead of a forced read-only policy, allowing a review prompt (or repository instructions it reads) to modify the checkout.

findings.title: Keep Codex execution read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: This wrapper runs Codex with opts.repoPath as its working directory. Removing the CLI-level read-only override allows configured sandbox policy to apply, including workspace-write or danger-full-access, so a prompt can modify the checkout being reviewed rather than only inspect it.

findings.title: Preserve the read-only sandbox for reviewer runs
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex launches Codex with cwd set to the repository being reviewed and supplies the review prompt on stdin. Removing `-s read-only` removes the enforced no-write boundary, so a write-enabled default sandbox (including after a Codex CLI upgrade) permits the subprocess to modify the reviewed repository.

findings.title: Generate the patch from the selected PR head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA is supplied and the checkout's HEAD differs from it, these commands review HEAD while postReview posts the result against headSha. Findings can therefore describe unrelated files or omit changes in the PR commit that receives the review.

findings.title: Diff from the PR merge base instead of the base tip
findings.whyItBreaks: If PR_BASE_SHA is the current target-branch tip and the PR head diverged before later target-branch commits, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes those target-only commits as reverse changes. Needlefish will review and may comment on deletions that are not part of the PR.

findings.title: Build the review diff from the PR head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: These commands now unconditionally compare baseSha with the checkout's HEAD, while headSha may be supplied independently via PR_HEAD_SHA and is still used to post the review/check. When Actions checks out a merge ref or any non-head commit, Needlefish reviews that checkout's changes but attaches the result to PR_HEAD_SHA, producing incorrect findings and inline-comment paths for the PR.

findings.title: Restore merge-base comparison for the PR patch
findings.whyItBreaks: `PR_BASE_SHA` denotes the base branch tip, which may have advanced after the PR branch forked. `git diff baseSha HEAD` compares endpoint trees, so it includes base-only changes (as removals) in both `patch` and `changedFiles`; the reviewer can assess unrelated code and attempt inline comments for files not changed by the PR. The previous merge-base range correctly isolated head-branch changes.

findings.title: Preserve literal payloads when replacing prompt placeholders
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace treats a string replacement specially: payload text such as `$&`, `$`` or `$'` is expanded using the matched placeholder or surrounding prompt. Since bundle JSON, candidate findings, and patches can legitimately contain these sequences, the generated review or critic prompt no longer contains the original data; `$&` alone injects the placeholder into JSON and can make the embedded bundle invalid.

findings.title: Preserve prompt payloads as literal text
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets `$&`, `$`` , `$'`, and `$$` in a string replacement. Bundle JSON, candidate findings, and especially raw patches can legitimately contain these sequences; their contents are then altered or expanded with surrounding prompt text before Codex sees them. The prior callback replacements inserted the payloads literally.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollars when injecting review data
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement. A bundle patch containing "$&" is inserted as "{{BUNDLE}}" instead of the literal patch content; the same corruption can affect candidate findings and the critic patch. Because PR-controlled source text is placed in these fields, a PR can cause the review or critic to receive altered or missing evidence.

findings.title: Pin fallback reviews to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review POST fails and the PR receives a new commit after `headSha` was captured, omitting `commit_id` makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the PR's most recent commit. The review body and event were computed from the older `headSha`, so a stale pass or change request is presented as a review of code that was never analyzed. Previously the fallback remained pinned to `headSha` and would fail rather than misrepresent the reviewed revision.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed commit ID in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: When the inline-comment POST fails, this fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub defaults that field to the PR's most recent commit, while this run computed its findings against headSha earlier. If a commit is pushed between those requests, a REQUEST_CHANGES review for the old diff is submitted against the new, unreviewed commit; meanwhile the check run remains associated with the old headSha.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the JSON submission fails, this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then targets the PR's latest commit rather than headSha, which was captured before the diff and review were computed. If a new commit is pushed while the review runs, the stale review can be posted as though it assessed the newer, unreviewed commit.

findings.title: Reject malformed finding fields instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously rejected malformed findings under its default strict mode. It now converts missing or invalid severity/category/location fields into a P1 bug at an empty file and line 0, so callers cannot distinguish invalid model output from a real finding and may act on a fabricated review result.

findings.title: Preserve the public strictness option
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using normalizeReview(raw, false) now fail to compile because the exported second parameter was removed. Those callers also lose the documented behavior that invalid findings are excluded in lenient mode.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating locations
findings.whyItBreaks: A finding missing file or lineStart now returns as a Finding with file="" and lineStart=0 rather than raising the malformed-output error. Callers cannot distinguish an invalid model response from a real finding, and may attempt to display or act on a nonexistent source location.

findings.title: Reject malformed finding fields
findings.whyItBreaks: An input such as `{ "severity": "P0" }` previously failed validation; it now produces a P0 finding with `file: ""`, `lineStart: 0`, and placeholder text. Consumers cannot distinguish malformed model output from a real finding and may report or act on a nonexistent P0.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict=false behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `strict` is a breaking exported API change. TypeScript callers using `normalizeReview(raw, false)` no longer compile; JavaScript callers silently change from dropping malformed findings to returning synthetic default findings.

findings.title: Keep the repository scope for manual PR ref resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before actions/checkout. Without -R "$REPO", gh pr view must infer a repository from the runner's working directory; a clean workspace has no checkout yet, causing ref resolution to fail (or a persistent self-hosted workspace can resolve against its stale repository). The subsequent checkout receives empty or wrong SHAs.

findings.title: Keep the repository explicit when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before actions/checkout. Without -R or GH_REPO, gh pr view resolves its repository from the current local Git repository; on a clean workspace it cannot resolve one, and on this self-hosted runner it can instead use a stale checkout. The requested PR's head/base outputs are therefore unavailable or can target the wrong repository.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository for manual ref lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before actions/checkout (line 42). `gh pr view <number>` resolves its repository from a local repository unless `--repo` or GH_REPO is supplied; there is no checkout or repository override at this point. The ref queries therefore fail or use stale self-hosted-runner repository state, leaving empty/wrong SHAs and preventing the requested PR from being reviewed.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output instead of defaulting it
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or malformed required fields now become empty strings or arrays. For example, `{ summary: "ok" }` becomes a review with zero findings and zero residual risks, indistinguishable from a valid clean review. The previous implementation threw on this invalid output, allowing callers to retry or surface the malformed response. Because normalizeReview is exported, this failure-as-empty contract ships even though this repository has no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs previously rejected for missing/invalid summary, findings, checked, or residual_risks now return empty defaults. A caller cannot distinguish an invalid review response from a genuine review with no findings, so malformed output can be treated as a clean review.

findings.title: Restore rejection of malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer previously threw for a non-object payload or missing required summary/findings/checked/residual_risks fields. It now returns an empty RawReview for all of those failures, making invalid model output indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings and an empty summary.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR's refs on manual runs
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no github.event.pull_request object. Consequently, checkout falls back to github.ref (the branch used to dispatch the workflow), BASE_REF falls back to main, and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are empty. The required pr_number is therefore ignored for revision selection, so manually reviewing a PR can analyze the wrong checkout and supplies no PR SHAs to the reviewer.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request payload. Thus checkout falls back to github.ref (the branch selected when dispatching, not necessarily the requested PR head), base fetch defaults to main, and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are empty. Dispatching the workflow for a PR targeting a non-main branch can therefore review the wrong revision or provide no diff bounds.

findings.title: Restore PR-head resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so this expression falls back to github.ref: the branch selected when starting the workflow, rather than the PR identified by inputs.pr_number. The review command still receives that requested PR number at line 47, so a normal manual run can analyze the workflow branch/default branch and publish its result to an unrelated PR.

findings.title: Preserve a buffer large enough for the full review diff
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal obtains the entire patch through git diff at line 100. Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default and terminates git when a repository diff exceeds that size, causing this helper to throw instead of producing a review. The prior 64 MiB limit explicitly supported substantially larger PRs.

findings.title: Preserve capacity for large Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB when omitted. The git helper is used for `git diff` at src/adapters/local.ts:100, so reviewing a diff larger than 1 MiB now terminates Git with a max-buffer error instead of constructing the review bundle. The prior 64 MiB limit supported those reviews.

findings.title: Preserve capacity for large git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. runLocal reads the complete base..HEAD patch through this helper at line 100, so any review diff exceeding 1 MiB now terminates with a maxBuffer error instead of producing a review. The prior 64 MiB limit explicitly supported substantially larger diffs.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, this reports the Needlefish check as neutral instead of failure. GitHub treats neutral as successful for required status checks, so a required Needlefish check can satisfy branch protection even though the review never completed.

findings.title: Report review errors as failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When review(), review posting, or check posting throws, the adapter now creates a completed neutral check even though it sets a nonzero process exit code. GitHub treats neutral as a non-failing check conclusion, so a required Needlefish check can cease blocking a PR whose review did not complete.

findings.title: Keep review errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a completed check with conclusion "neutral" as successful for required status checks. Therefore, when the review throws, this posts a Needlefish check that can satisfy branch protection even though the review did not run to completion; the prior "failure" conclusion correctly blocked that path.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer executable on a trusted revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The only checkout is now the PR head, and the final step runs its src/cli.ts. A same-repository PR can modify that file to submit a false review or create arbitrary check results using GH_TOKEN, which has pull-requests: write and checks: write permissions. The prior separate checkout prevented the review target from controlling the reviewer.

The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout trusted
findings.whyItBreaks: The checkout at lines 43-47 is the PR head, and this command executes its src/cli.ts. A same-repository PR can modify that CLI (or its install-time dependencies at line 51) to forge review output or use GH_TOKEN to write PR comments/checks. Because the job runs on a self-hosted runner, it also executes arbitrary PR code on that runner. The removed main checkout was the boundary preventing the reviewed change from controlling its reviewer.

The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore the trusted checkout before running the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is checked out at lines 43-47, then its own src/cli.ts is executed with GH_TOKEN at line 56. For any same-repository PR allowed by the job condition, an attacker can modify cli.ts to use the token's pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions, or execute arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner. The previous workflow isolated the untrusted target from a main-branch reviewer checkout.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.

findings.title: Canonicalize severity before validating it
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously accepted values such as " p0 " and "p1" by trimming and uppercasing them. The new exact-match check rejects those inputs and returns P3, so a highest-severity finding can be emitted as the lowest severity in the normalized public review result.

findings.title: Preserve canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw JSON and passes each finding to this function at src/shared/schema.ts:132. Inputs such as "p0" or " P2 " were previously canonicalized to P0/P2, but now fail the exact-match check and are silently downgraded to P3, changing review severity.

findings.title: Preserve severity normalization before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external payloads and passes each raw finding here. A payload severity such as " p2 " or "p2" previously normalized to P2, but now fails the exact-membership check and is silently emitted as P3, changing the reported severity.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit sanitized env, spawnSync inherits process.env, exposing GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN to the Codex subprocess. The prior revision explicitly removed all three credentials, so an untrusted prompt or repository-influenced command executed by Codex can now use or exfiltrate the caller's GitHub token.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without the explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env. A Codex run handling an untrusted review prompt can read GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN through its command environment and return the secret in its output, despite the read-only filesystem sandbox.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit environment allow/scrub logic makes `codex exec` inherit `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The child agent receives a prompt and can invoke subprocesses, so untrusted repository/prompt content can cause these credentials to be read and returned in agent output or used for unauthorized GitHub API operations.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for self-hosted execution
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job-level fork guard makes every fork PR reach checkout of its head SHA and then execute `pnpm install` and `tsx src/cli.ts` on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can change package metadata, dependencies, or src/cli.ts to run arbitrary commands on that runner and access its environment, workspace, and any credentials available to it.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed condition previously restricted this job to same-repository PRs. Fork PRs now check out their attacker-controlled head SHA (line 23), install its dependency graph (line 28), and execute its CLI/source (line 34) on a self-hosted runner. That permits arbitrary code execution on the persistent runner and can expose its workspace, runner credentials, and any credentials available to later trusted jobs.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull_request events now run this job. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled head SHA and executes both its dependency installation and src/cli.ts on a persistent self-hosted runner, allowing an external PR author to execute arbitrary code and compromise the runner environment.

findings.title: Preserve valid zero-duration runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" was previously accepted and made the SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL grace period or post-SIGKILL give-up delay effectively immediate. It now falls back to 5000ms or 2000ms, respectively, so existing configurations that require prompt timeout completion wait seconds longer.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, an explicit value of "0" was accepted. It now falls back silently: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 becomes 5000 ms before SIGKILL, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 becomes 2000 ms before timeout resolution. Existing deployments that intentionally configured immediate escalation or completion change behavior on upgrade.

findings.title: Keep deep review coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews retain only six mapped hotspots. Removing the tail-coverage hotspot means any changed file omitted by the mapper or beyond those selected hotspots is never sent to deep review; the critic receives only patch statistics, so it cannot inspect the skipped diff.

findings.title: Preserve blocked residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each successful deep review can return residual risks, including blocking uncertainty, but the merged candidate now replaces them with an empty array. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a deep review that reported a blocker from one that reported no risk, allowing the final verdict to lose a required block.

findings.title: Restore deep coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews retain only six mapped hotspots. Removing the tail-coverage hotspot means files mapped to later hotspots, or omitted by the mapper, are never supplied to a deep review. The critic receives only the merged findings and patch stat, so it can return a clean review without any examination of those changes.

findings.title: Carry deep-pass residual risks into the final verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep reviewer can return a blocking residual risk, but this code replaces all such signals with an empty array before invoking the critic. The critic and deriveVerdict consequently cannot distinguish an unresolved blocker from a fully reviewed hotspot, allowing a PASS despite a deep pass explicitly lacking evidence.

findings.title: Restore coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapper-selected hotspots are deep-reviewed. Removed tail coverage means a changed file omitted by the mapper, or placed in a hotspot beyond that limit, is never reviewed and no residual risk reports the omission.

findings.title: Keep deep-review failures fail-closed
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed runCodex response from any one hotspot now escapes reviewLarge and rejects the entire review. Previously that hotspot produced a blocking residual risk while the remaining hotspots were still reviewed.

findings.title: Preserve deep-review residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: Residual risks returned by successful deep reviewers, including blocks:true risks for unresolved review evidence, are replaced with an empty array before the critic runs. The critic and final verdict therefore cannot distinguish a fully reviewed PR from one with a blocking unresolved surface.

findings.title: Forward focus guidance to large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: For bundles routed to reviewLarge (patches over 30,000 characters or more than 10 files), the map prompt no longer receives bundle.focus, and the deep prompt no longer substitutes {{FOCUS}}. A caller's requested review focus is therefore ignored only for large PRs, despite being preserved by reviewSmall.

findings.title: Preserve review directives in the large-review path
findings.whyItBreaks: When a bundle exceeds the large-review threshold, reviewLarge now omits focus and deep from the mapper input, and focus is also omitted from every deep-review prompt. The same Bundle is passed intact to reviewSmall, so a caller's requested review focus/depth works for small PRs but is silently ignored for large PRs—the cases most likely to need it.

findings.title: Preserve focus in each large-review deep prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: When a bundle exceeds the large-review threshold, review() dispatches to reviewLarge(), but the deep prompt no longer receives bundle.focus. A caller-provided focus instruction is therefore honored for small reviews (which serialize the complete bundle) but dropped for large reviews, causing the review agent to inspect arbitrary mapped hotspots rather than the requested area.

findings.title: Normalize carry when rounded seconds reach 60
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500 ms, minutes is computed as 1 and rounded remainder seconds as 60, so review output displays "1m 60s" instead of the normalized "2m 0s". The prior implementation rounded total seconds before deriving minutes and handled this carry correctly.

findings.title: Normalize seconds after rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500 ms, minutes is computed as 1 while the remainder rounds to 60, so rendered review statistics show `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`.

findings.title: Normalize rounded seconds before formatting
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations with a remaining fraction of 59.5–59.999 seconds, `Math.round` produces `60` after minutes have already been calculated. For example, 119500ms renders as `1m 60s` rather than `2m 0s`; this is emitted in the public markdown review output.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger("0", label) now returns 0 even though both its exported name and its error contract promise a positive integer. Callers can therefore receive a value outside the stated public contract.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: With parsed=0, `parsed < 0` is false, so this exported function returns zero despite its name and error contract requiring a positive integer. Consumers can therefore receive an invalid non-positive value without an error.

findings.title: Restore positive-only validation
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger("0", label) now returns 0 even though its exported name and thrown-error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers can rely on this parser to enforce values greater than zero and will receive an invalid zero instead.
